sections.overview: Papilio aegeus is a large swallowtail native to eastern Australia and nearby islands; cultivated citrus provides additional larval food in settled areas.
sections.identification: Males are mainly black and white with a red hindwing spot; browner females bear broader pale markings and red crescents, so the sexes look quite different.
sections.habitat: It inhabits gardens, woodland and forests where host plants grow, and is common in some eastern Australian suburbs.
sections.diet: Caterpillars feed on citrus and other Rutaceae, including Australian native plants; recorded hosts vary by region.
sections.behavior: Young caterpillars resemble bird droppings; older larvae can expose a red, foul-smelling osmeterium when threatened, and males defend territories.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs on host plants and larvae pass through several growth stages before pupating; a single development time is not assumed for all conditions.
sections.ecology: It shares the genus Papilio with the Dainty Swallowtail, P. anactus; both use citrus, though their recorded host lists are not identical.
sections.conservation: It remains widespread in eastern Australia and can benefit from cultivated citrus; no global assessment or population trend was found in the consulted sources.
